Black Girl Sunscreen Turns 10: A Decade of Making Sun Protection for Melanin-Rich Skin
 Jameelah "Just Jay" Wilkerson

 Send an email

 Alpantex / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0) Ten years ago, Shontay Lundy looked at the sunscreen aisle and saw a problem nobody in the beauty industry seemed willing to fix. The products on the shelves were not made with her skin in mind. They left a chalky white cast on deeper tones, and the message underneath was clear: sun protection was not really meant for Black and Brown women.
 So she built the product herself. Black Girl Sunscreen, founded in 2016, turns 10 this year — and this week the brand is marking the milestone with an anniversary celebration in Los Angeles, a new partnership with the Melanoma Research Alliance, and a look ahead to a second decade that Lundy says is about much more than selling sunscreen.
 A Decade in the Sun
 The anniversary celebration, called A Decade in the Sun, takes place November 20, 2026, in Los Angeles, bringing together the partners, supporters and individuals who have contributed to the brand’s journey. The event is supported by JPMorganChase, Rosenthal Capital Group and Planned Parenthood — organizations representing different but meaningful relationships in the Black Girl Sunscreen story, from financial infrastructure to community health.
 What began as a mission to create sunscreen specifically with melanin-rich skin in mind has grown into a nationally recognized brand with a presence in more than 12,000 doors across major retailers and an expanding international footprint. The brand is stocked at Target, Ulta, CVS and Walgreens, and Lundy has taken its message to Good Morning America and The View, along with her podcast, Shamelessly Shontay.
 “A decade in the sun has taught me that this was never just about a product. It was about making sure we’re included in the conversation about our own health,” Lundy said. “Partnering with the Melanoma Research Alliance is the next chapter of that mission, and I’m grateful to every partner and customer who has believed in what we’re building.”
 The Problem She Set Out to Solve
 When Lundy launched the brand in 2016, the sunscreen industry was still framed through a narrow lens. For millions of people with melanated skin, sunscreen was not just inconvenient — it was something the industry had never truly considered. The white cast was the most visible symptom, but the deeper issue was exclusion: an entire category of products designed as if darker skin did not need protection, or did not deserve products made for it.
 Black Girl Sunscreen set out to solve the most persistent frustration in the category head-on. Its formulas were built to disappear into melanin-rich skin without the ashy residue, and the brand’s message was unapologetic from the start: Black women belong at the center of the sun care conversation.
 Nearly a decade later, that single conviction has built a full product ecosystem — lotions, sprays, lip SPF, kids’ formulas, and the newest launch, the Sun Ready Stick SPF 30. The brand marked the anniversary with a limited-edition version of its original SPF 30 moisturizing sunscreen, listed at $23.99 on its website, with a founder’s note thanking the customers who believed in the brand from the beginning.
 The timing reflects a market that has finally caught up to what Lundy saw in 2016. Industry research valued the global sun care market at more than $15 billion in 2025, with expectations of roughly $16.6 billion in 2026 — growth driven in part by consumers who were long overlooked finally being served.
 A New Partnership With Real Stakes
 As Black Girl Sunscreen enters its second decade, the company is announcing a partnership with the Melanoma Research Alliance, a nonprofit dedicated to advancing melanoma research, prevention and treatment. Lundy recently joined the Alliance’s Leadership Council, deepening her commitment to its mission.
 The partnership, extending through September 2027, will focus on raising awareness about melanoma, supporting research and expanding conversations around sun safety and prevention. Through education, consumer engagement and collaborative initiatives, the two organizations aim to reinforce the importance of daily sun protection and increase awareness among communities that have historically been underserved in conversations about skin health.
 The stakes are not abstract. “Melanoma affects over 100,000 people every year and nearly everyone knows someone impacted,” said Dana Deighton, the Alliance’s Director of Communications & Engagement. “Facts matter and the more we educate people about melanoma prevention, early detection, and their unique risk factors — no matter the skin color — the more lives we save. That’s why the Melanoma Research Alliance is honored to partner with Black Girl Sunscreen, an early innovator when it comes to making sun safety relevant to people with skin of color.”
 That last point matters. The persistent myth that melanin-rich skin does not need sun protection has real consequences. Melanin provides some natural protection, but it does not prevent sun damage, and unprotected exposure remains one of the leading triggers of hyperpigmentation, dark marks and uneven tone for deeper skin — alongside the more serious risks that too often get diagnosed late in Black patients. Dermatologists recommend daily broad-spectrum SPF of 30 or higher, and the message Lundy has carried for a decade is that protection is a daily habit, not a beach-day accessory.
 Beauty Founder of the Year
 The anniversary arrives alongside a personal honor for Lundy. She was named Beauty Founder of the Year at the 2026 Melanin Beauty Awards, an recognition that landed just days before the anniversary announcement. In interviews around the award, she has been candid about what the decade cost and what it built — and about the community work that runs alongside the business.
 That work is deliberately small-scale and personal. The brand fields thousands of emails from people who love its products, many of them small asks: a Pilates class, a church gathering, a university celebration, a dermatologist’s office. Black Girl Sunscreen sends product. Lundy shows up at community charity events and reminds people to get their skin checked. It is the kind of grassroots presence that a brand cannot buy, and it is a large part of why the company’s tenth anniversary feels like a community milestone rather than a corporate one.
 “Ten years later, the core of Black Girl Sunscreen still means the same thing even as the business and I evolve,” Lundy has said of the brand’s identity. The statement is a mission, not a slogan: putting Black women at the center of a conversation the beauty industry spent decades having without them.
 Looking Toward 2027
 As Black Girl Sunscreen looks toward 2027 and beyond, the company remains focused on expanding its reach, strengthening its partnerships and continuing the mission that inspired its founding. The Melanoma Research Alliance partnership gives that mission a clinical backbone, pairing a brand that made sun care culturally relevant with a research organization working on prevention, early detection and treatment.
 For Hype readers, the lesson of the last ten years is simple. Representation in beauty is not about a shade range or a marketing campaign. It is about whether a product was designed with you in mind in the first place — and whether the industry around it treats your health as worth protecting. Shontay Lundy spent a decade proving that it is. The next decade, she says, is about making sure nobody has to prove it again.
